title: Who Is Prophet Muhammad ﷺ?
subtitle: His life, the evidence for his mission, and the questions a seeker should ask
summary: Muhammad ﷺ proclaimed the Quran in seventh-century Arabia and taught worship of God alone. Muslims identify him as God's final messenger, not as divine. His case rests on the Quran together with a critically read life: testimony to his character, refusal of personal deification, perseverance, and the community he formed. Neither political success nor sincerity alone proves prophethood.

seo.metaTitle: Who Is Prophet Muhammad? A Beginner's Biography
seo.metaDescription: A sourced introduction to Muhammad's life and the Muslim case for his mission, including character evidence, source limits, and serious objections.

sections.title: A Human Messenger With a Claim to Test
sections.body:
Muhammad ﷺ is the seventh-century Arabian prophet through whom Muslims believe God revealed the Quran. The standard Islamic chronology places his birth around 570, the beginning of revelation around 610, migration to Medina in 622, and death in 632. He called people to worship Allah alone and to prepare for judgment.

Why believe his claim? Muslims point to the Quran and to the fit between its message and his life. That is more than admiration for an influential leader, but it also requires more care than repeating every favorable story as certain history.

sections.title: The First Revelation: Testimony, Not an Unexamined Legend
sections.body:
The traditional biography places Muhammad among Quraysh in Mecca, working in trade and married to Khadijah. [Sahih al-Bukhari 3](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3) describes his first revelatory experience as frightening, not a triumphant announcement of personal greatness. Khadijah reassures him by recalling his care for relatives, vulnerable people, and guests.

This is concrete testimony to the character remembered by his household. It also gives a reason Muslims reject the picture of a casual inventor seeking attention. But it is transmitted within the Muslim community in a later collection, not a recording made in the cave. Its authenticity must be assessed as hadith, and sincere fear would not by itself distinguish revelation from a sincere mistaken experience.

sections.title: From Persecution to Public Responsibility
sections.body:
The migration to Medina in 622 changed a persecuted movement into a community with public authority. The standard biography includes the battles of Badr and Uhud, the siege of Medina, the Hudaybiyyah truce, and entry into Mecca before his death in 632. These events matter because prophecy here is not only private spirituality: it involves treaties, law, conflict, and the use of power.

In the [Hudaybiyyah account](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2731), negotiation and an unwelcome compromise are part of his leadership. Muslims see patient commitment rather than a mission dependent on instant victory. A critic can instead see skilled statecraft. Military or political success proves neither divine approval nor fraud; the moral quality of the mission and the Quran's claim must carry that judgment.

sections.title: Character Is Tested Where Power Is Closest
sections.body:
A public reputation should be checked against conduct at home. Aisha reports that Muhammad did not strike a woman or servant ([Sahih Muslim 2328a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:2328a)). This is specific evidence relevant to how he treated people under his authority, not merely a label such as 'merciful.' Quran 4:19 commands honorable treatment of wives, while 33:6 gives his wives a special status in the believing community.

The marriage reports also raise serious questions, especially about Aisha. The dominant traditional Sunni reports, including [Bukhari 5134](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5134), give a young age; alternative reconstructions exist but should not be presented as if they had displaced those reports. Historical explanation is not permission to ignore consent, harm, or obligations toward children today. A full answer needs the sources and the ethical question, not a convenient rewritten biography.

sections.title: What About War and Other Hard Reports?
sections.body:
Muhammad was also a commander and judge. An honest introduction must leave room for examining reports about captives, punishments, and Banu Qurayza. The first task is to establish which version is being discussed and how well it is transmitted. The next is to ask about responsibility, proportionality, treaty obligations, and the difference between explanation and moral justification.

A serious objection is that the sources are largely written by believers and can idealize their founder. The answer is not that believers cannot transmit history, nor that every report must be true. Compare the earliest Quranic witness, different chains and wordings, and the historical setting. A difficult report should neither be erased because it is uncomfortable nor accepted in its most sensational version. The [early preservation study](/articles/early-islamic-preservation) explains what authentication can and cannot establish.

sections.title: One Refusal That Bears on His Claim
sections.body:
Quran 3:144 expressly places Muhammad among mortal messengers. Quran 33:40 identifies him as the final prophet; it states Islam's claim rather than independently proving it.

There is also a revealing report: when an eclipse coincided with his son Ibrahim's death, Muhammad rejected the suggestion that the sky was responding to the death ([Sahih al-Bukhari 1043](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1043)). If reliable, this is evidence against exploiting a ready-made supernatural tribute to his family. The testimony comes through later Muslim transmission, so a skeptic may question its origin. Even with that qualification, it fits the Quran's refusal to make its messenger divine and gives the claim a concrete moral shape.

sections.title: From Sincerity to Prophethood
sections.body:
The strongest alternative to prophethood is not simply a dishonest man. A sincere religious reformer could teach monotheism, show courage, and build a community. Sincerity is therefore relevant but insufficient. Nor can a modern reader responsibly diagnose Muhammad with a medical condition from distant reports.

The Muslim conclusion joins the evidence: the Quran's account of God and moral life, its recited form, early access to its text, and a life whose authority directs people beyond the messenger to God. Authenticated character reports add weight; conquest or popularity alone adds none. Muslims judge revelation the best explanation of that whole pattern. The [case for the Quran](/articles/why-the-quran) develops the part of the argument that character alone cannot supply.

sections.title: What Following Him Would Mean
sections.body:
The Sunnah is Muhammad's example, known through reports that must be authenticated and interpreted. Following him means worshiping the God he worshiped and learning truthfulness, mercy, responsibility, and justice—not treating any later action by a Muslim ruler as automatically prophetic.

Read [Why the Quran?](/articles/why-the-quran) next, with these questions in view: does the message deserve the authority it claims, do the strongest objections receive a real answer, and is prophethood a better explanation than the serious alternatives? A respectful inquiry can be candid about all three.

quranVerses.arabic: وَمَا مُحَمَّدٌ إِلَّا رَسُولٌۭ قَدْ خَلَتْ مِن قَبْلِهِ ٱلرُّسُلُ ۚ أَفَإِي۟ن مَّاتَ أَوْ قُتِلَ ٱنقَلَبْتُمْ عَلَىٰٓ أَعْقَٰبِكُمْ ۚ وَمَن يَنقَلِبْ عَلَىٰ عَقِبَيْهِ فَلَن يَضُرَّ ٱللَّهَ شَيْـًۭٔا ۗ وَسَيَجْزِى ٱللَّهُ ٱلشَّٰكِرِينَ
quranVerses.translation: Muhammad is not but a messenger. [Other] messengers have passed on before him. So if he was to die or be killed, would you turn back on your heels [to unbelief]? And he who turns back on his heels will never harm Allah at all; but Allah will reward the grateful.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: ٱلنَّبِىُّ أَوْلَىٰ بِٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ مِنْ أَنفُسِهِمْ ۖ وَأَزْوَٰجُهُۥٓ أُمَّهَٰتُهُمْ ۗ وَأُو۟لُوا۟ ٱلْأَرْحَامِ بَعْضُهُمْ أَوْلَىٰ بِبَعْضٍۢ فِى كِتَٰبِ ٱللَّهِ مِنَ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَٱلْمُهَٰجِرِينَ إِلَّآ أَن تَفْعَلُوٓا۟ إِلَىٰٓ أَوْلِيَآئِكُم مَّعْرُوفًۭا ۚ كَانَ ذَٰلِكَ فِى ٱلْكِتَٰبِ مَسْطُورًۭا
quranVerses.translation: The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves, and his wives are [in the position of] their mothers. And those of [blood] relationship are more entitled [to inheritance] in the decree of Allah than the [other] believers and the emigrants, except that you may do to your close associates a kindness [through bequest]. That was in the Book inscribed.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ لَا يَحِلُّ لَكُمْ أَن تَرِثُوا۟ ٱلنِّسَآءَ كَرْهًۭا ۖ وَلَا تَعْضُلُوهُنَّ لِتَذْهَبُوا۟ بِبَعْضِ مَآ ءَاتَيْتُمُوهُنَّ إِلَّآ أَن يَأْتِينَ بِفَٰحِشَةٍۢ مُّبَيِّنَةٍۢ ۚ وَعَاشِرُوهُنَّ بِٱلْمَعْرُوفِ ۚ فَإِن كَرِهْتُمُوهُنَّ فَعَسَىٰٓ أَن تَكْرَهُوا۟ شَيْـًۭٔا وَيَجْعَلَ ٱللَّهُ فِيهِ خَيْرًۭا كَثِيرًۭا
quranVerses.translation: O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion. And do not make difficulties for them in order to take [back] part of what you gave them unless they commit a clear immorality. And live with them in kindness. For if you dislike them - perhaps you dislike a thing and Allah makes therein much good.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: مَّا كَانَ مُحَمَّدٌ أَبَآ أَحَدٍۢ مِّن رِّجَالِكُمْ وَلَٰكِن رَّسُولَ ٱللَّهِ وَخَاتَمَ ٱلنَّبِيِّۦنَ ۗ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ بِكُلِّ شَىْءٍ عَلِيمًۭا
quranVerses.translation: Muhammad is not the father of [any] one of your men, but [he is] the Messenger of Allah and last of the prophets. And ever is Allah, of all things, Knowing.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

faq.question: What does ﷺ mean?
faq.answer: It represents an Arabic prayer for God's peace and blessings upon Muhammad. It expresses respect, not a claim that he is divine.

faq.question: Do Muslims worship Muhammad?
faq.answer: No. Worship belongs to Allah alone. Quran 3:144 describes Muhammad as a mortal messenger, and Muslim devotion to him must remain within that boundary.

faq.question: Does good character prove prophethood?
faq.answer: No. It bears on sincerity and trustworthiness, but a sincere person could still be mistaken. Muslims combine the character evidence with the case for the Quran and the wider mission.

faq.question: How early are the sources for his life?
faq.answer: The Quran is the earliest central witness to the proclamation. Biography and hadith provide much more detail through later transmitted texts. Each report's date, chain, wording, and corroboration matter; a later collection is neither a contemporary recording nor evidence that all its material was invented late.

faq.question: Where can I ask about Aisha or warfare?
faq.answer: These questions deserve specific sources and a complete ethical answer. Use the site's Claims Against Islam discussion alongside qualified scholarship, and do not mistake this short introduction for a resolution of every disputed episode.
